# 角色
你是一名资深的医学与人工智能领域审稿专家，熟悉Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics 的学术标准与评审流程。你曾在人工智能医学交叉领域发表或评审多篇高质量论文，熟悉科研论文的学术规范、逻辑结构、创新性与方法学严谨性要求。

# 审稿任务
请你严格、系统地对以下论文进行审稿，论文主题为“人工智能（尤其是大语言模型，LLM）与生物医学的结合”。你的目标是从多个角度提供专业、学术化的审稿意见，帮助作者改进论文质量，以达到北大核心期刊的发表标准。

# 审稿维度
请从以下方面系统性地进行审阅与评估：
1. 整体评价与科学价值  
   - 论文选题的创新性与前沿性是否突出？  
   - 是否具有明确的科研意义和社会/医学价值？  

2. 内容质量与逻辑性  
   - 研究问题是否明确，论证是否严谨？  
   - 文章结构是否清晰（摘要、引言、方法、结果、讨论、结论）？  
   - 逻辑链是否顺畅、论点是否有数据支撑？  

3. 方法与实验设计  
   - 模型、算法、数据来源与实验设计是否合理？  
   - 是否具备可重复性与科学性？  
   - 方法是否符合伦理及科研规范？  

4. 结果与讨论部分  
   - 结果展示是否清晰、完整？  
   - 图表、数据分析是否规范（如均值±SD、显著性标注等）？  
   - 讨论是否结合最新文献，是否能合理解释结果？  
   - 是否分析了研究局限与未来改进方向？  

5. 语言与格式规范  
   - 是否符合北大核心学术期刊写作规范？  
   - 英文摘要、关键词、图表说明是否准确？  
   - 是否存在语法、术语不一致或引用不规范的问题？  

6. 总体建议（必须输出）  
   请用以下分类之一总结你的总体结论：  
   ✅ 接受（Accept）：内容完整，质量高，可直接发表。  
   🟡 小修后接收（Minor Revision）：结构合理但需少量修改。  
   🟠 大修后重审（Major Revision）：存在逻辑或方法学问题，需大幅修改。 
   🔴 拒稿（Reject）：存在严重缺陷或学术质量不达标。  

# 输出格式
请严格按照以下结构输出审稿意见：
一、总体评价  
（简要评价论文选题意义、创新性与整体质量）

二、主要优点  
（列出论文在理论、方法或应用方面的亮点）

三、存在问题与修改建议  
（从逻辑、方法、实验、数据、讨论、语言规范等角度逐条指出）

四、编辑建议  
（给出你的总体判断：接受/小修/大修/拒稿，并简述理由）

# 输出要求
- 语气：专业、学术、客观  
- 格式：条理清晰，分点列述  
- 内容：针对性强、可操作性高  
- 若发现重大逻辑或伦理问题，请明确指出并说明原因。

# 输入内容
论文全文如下（或节选）：
"""
{在此粘贴论文正文或摘要}
"""

IEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 1

1



IEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 2

From Clinical Features to Raw Signals in 12-Lead
ECG: A Patient-Level Benchmark with External

Validation and Targeted Perturbation Analysis
Anonymous

Abstract—Background: Large-scale ECG classification models
require robust patient-level validation to assess generalizability.
However, different model classes may extract different informa-
tion pathways for the same cardiac condition, and whether deep
learning exploits clinically meaningful signal segments remains
underexplored.

Methods: We conducted patient-level held-out validation on
CODE-15% (345,797 samples, 233,771 patients) for 5 cardiac
conditions: 1st-degree AV block (1AVB), complete right/left
bundle branch blocks (CRBBB/CLBBB), sinus bradycardia
(SBRAD), and atrial fibrillation (AFIB). We compared three
approaches: (1) XGBoost with simple summary features—rhythm
statistics (RR intervals, HRV, 14D) and crude amplitude statistics
(per-lead mean/std/min/max, 84D); (2) XGBoost with Clinical-
MVP features adding AV conduction timing (PR interval, QRS
duration, QRS axis, R/S ratio) and signal quality metrics (110D
total); and (3) 1D ResNet on raw 12-lead signals. Patient-level
splitting (60/20/20) prevented data leakage. To investigate model
reliance on specific signal segments, we performed three per-
turbation experiments with matched controls: PR-window occlu-
sion (160ms) targeting 1AVB, QRS-complex occlusion targeting
BBB, and RR-interval regularization targeting AFIB. Statistical
robustness was assessed via multi-seed training, bootstrap CIs
(n = 1000), and Holm-Bonferroni corrected pairwise model
comparisons. Cross-dataset feature validation was performed
by training XGBoost on PTB-XL+ 12SL features (783D) using
official patient-level folds.

Results: Feature ablation revealed that information path-
way importance depends on model class: rhythm features
(14D) excelled at SBRAD/AFIB, amplitude features (84D) ex-
celled at BBB, but 1AVB detection remained weak (F1=0.0808,
AUROC=0.682) due to missing PR-interval timing. Clinical-
MVP features (110D) substantially improved 1AVB (F1=0.447,
AUROC=0.961) and overall Micro-F1 to 0.654 (+27.7% vs simple
features). 1D ResNet achieved Micro-F1=0.736±0.003, outper-
forming both feature-based approaches; SE-ResNet (channel
attention) yielded no detectable improvement (Micro-F1=0.736,
∆ =+0.0002, all per-disease ∆F1 within multi-seed variance).
A lightweight 1D transformer (1.4M parameters, identical conv
stem and data splits) underperformed ResNet substantially
(Micro-F1=0.605, ∆ = −0.131), indicating that ResNet’s con-
volutional inductive bias is better suited for ECG signals than
patch-based self-attention at comparable parameter counts. Per-
turbation experiments provided evidence consistent with disease-
specific model reliance: PR-window occlusion degraded 1AVB
AUROC from 0.985 to 0.760 (∆ = −0.225) with anatomical
specificity (ST control: ∆ = −0.005); QRS occlusion degraded
CRBBB AUROC from 0.991 to 0.494 (∆ = −0.497) and
CLBBB from 0.991 to 0.645 (∆ = −0.346); RR regularization
showed an inconclusive effect on AFIB (AUROC 0.980→0.973,
∆ = −0.007, indistinguishable from beat-permutation control
∆ = −0.008). Cross-dataset PTB-XL+ XGBoost (783D) achieved

Manuscript submitted for blind review to IEEE Journal of Biomedical and
Health Informatics.

Micro-F1=0.777. Frozen-model external validation of CODE-
trained ResNet on PTB-XL raw signals was performed using a
3-tier framework: the primary endpoint—strict frozen transfer
with no target-domain tuning—achieved Micro-F1=0.571 (AU-
ROC preserved: 1AVB=0.937, CRBBB=0.995, CLBBB=0.995,
SBRAD=0.950, AFIB=0.972). Threshold recalibration on fold
9 (calibrated tier, Micro-F1=0.681 [0.651, 0.711]) recovered
substantial performance, while the best-possible tier (oracle
thresholds, Micro-F1=0.694) established the upper bound. The
strict-frozen-to-calibrated gap reflects threshold miscalibration,
not model degradation (AUROC identical across tiers). CLBBB
transferred near-perfectly (∆F1= −0.010) while 1AVB showed
the largest domain gap (∆F1= −0.124). PR>200ms rule
baseline using NeuroKit2 ECG delineation (AUROC=0.783,
sensitivity=0.873) showed that PR prolongation is highly sensitive
for 1AVB, while ResNet (AUROC=0.937, ∆ = +0.154, DeLong
p < 10−6) provides additional discriminative information beyond
PR interval alone. Residual label circularity cannot be defini-
tively excluded without physician adjudication of CODE labels.
Bootstrap CIs and DeLong tests provided statistical evidence for
ResNet superiority across all diseases.

Conclusions: Information pathways in ECG classification
are model-dependent: different model classes extract differ-
ent clinically meaningful signal channels from the same task.
Rhythm features suffice for rhythm disorders in XGBoost, but
ResNet captures AFIB through atrial activity (P/f-wave region)
rather than RR irregularity alone (atrial inpainting ∆AUROC=
−0.112 on PTB-XL, −0.142 on CODE; p = 0.0002 for both
datasets vs ST control). Clinical-MVP features incorporating
timing measurements closed > 50% of the ResNet perfor-
mance gap for 1AVB. Two perturbation pathways showed large,
anatomically specific effects: PR timing→1AVB (∆AUROC=
−0.225) and QRS morphology→BBB (∆AUROC= −0.497/-
0.346), whileRR→AFIB was inconclusive (∆ = −0.007). Frozen-
model external validation on PTB-XL raw signals preserved
AUROC> 0.93 across all diseases on human-validated labels
(strict frozen Micro-F1=0.571; calibrated=0.681). The transfer
gap pattern was consistent with the perturbation hierarchy,
suggesting an observational association between identified path-
ways and generalization. These findings provide a perturbation-
supported, externally-tested framework linking deep learning
behavior to clinically interpretable signal segments, with pathway
alignment rather than model size explaining performance and
transfer behavior.

Index Terms—ECG classification, patient-level validation, deep
learning, feature engineering, perturbation analysis, cross-dataset
validation, occlusion analysis

I. INTRODUCTION

A. Background

Electrocardiogram (ECG) classification using machine
learning has shown promise for automated cardiac diagnosis



IEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 3

[1]–[3]. However, most studies focus on internal validation or
small held-out cohorts, limiting generalizability assessment.
Furthermore, different cardiac conditions require different in-
formation pathways: rhythm disorders depend on RR-interval
patterns, conduction blocks require morphology analysis, and
atrioventricular blocks need precise PR-interval measurement.
Whether deep learning models rely on these clinically mean-
ingful signal segments or exploit spurious correlations remains
an open question.

B. Related Work

Large-scale ECG datasets: PTB-XL [4] (21k samples)
and CODE-15% [5] (345k samples) enabled large-scale val-
idation studies. Ribeiro et al. [1] achieved cardiologist-level
performance on CODE using 1D ResNet-based architecture.
However, these studies focused on aggregate performance
without investigating disease-specific feature requirements or
validating learned mechanisms.

Handcrafted ECG features: PTB-XL+ [6] introduced 166
handcrafted features including morphology, rhythm, and tim-
ing measurements (QRS duration, PR interval, QT interval,
axis, fiducial points). While comprehensive, the feature set re-
quires complex fiducial point detection (P/QRS/T onset/offset),
which can be fragile on noisy signals. Our work systemat-
ically compares simple summary features against clinically-
informed features incorporating AV conduction timing, iden-
tifying which information pathways are essential for each
condition.

Deep learning for ECG: Recent work [1], [2], [7] demon-
strated that end-to-end deep learning on raw signals achieves
strong performance. However, the mechanisms by which deep
learning succeeds where handcrafted features fail remain un-
derexplored. Our work bridges this gap through both feature
engineering (adding timing features to close the gap) and
perturbation-based analysis (PR-window occlusion to inves-
tigate learned mechanisms).

Patient-level validation: Most ECG classification studies
report internal validation or small held-out cohorts. Our work
provides rigorous patient-level held-out validation on 345k
samples, with detailed failure-mode analysis, perturbation-
based interpretability experiments, and multi-seed statistical
robustness assessment.

C. Motivation

The CODE-15% dataset [5] provides a large-scale Brazil-
ian ECG cohort (345,797 samples) for patient-level held-
out validation. Unlike prior work focusing solely on model
performance, we investigate why certain conditions fail with
specific feature sets, whether adding clinically-informed fea-
tures closes the gap, and whether deep learning relies on
clinically meaningful signal segments, providing interpretable
insights into ECG classification.

D. Contributions

1) Model-dependent information pathways: Provided ev-
idence through ablation studies that different model

classes extract different clinically meaningful signal
channels from the same ECG task—pathway alignment,
not model size alone, explains performance differences.

2) Failure-mode analysis: Quantified why 1AVB detection
fails with simple features (missing PR-interval timing)
through detailed score distribution and clinical mecha-
nism analysis.

3) Clinical-MVP baseline: Showed that adding AV con-
duction timing features (PR interval, QRS duration, QRS
axis) closes > 50% of the 1AVB performance gap,
supporting the timing information hypothesis.

4) Multi-pathway perturbation evidence: Three perturba-
tion experiments with matched controls provide evidence
consistent with ResNet relying on clinically meaningful
signal segments: strong effects for PR timing→1AVB
(AUROC 0.985→0.760, ∆ = −0.225) and QRS
morphology→BBB (CRBBB AUROC 0.991→0.494,
∆ = −0.497; CLBBB 0.991→0.645, ∆ = −0.346),
and an inconclusive effect for RR irregularity→AFIB
(AUROC 0.980→0.973, ∆ = −0.007, indistinguishable
from beat-permutation control ∆ = −0.008).

5) Frozen-model external validation with 3-tier frame-
work: CODE-trained ResNet transferred to PTB-XL
raw signals in three tiers. Primary endpoint—strict
frozen (CODE thresholds, no target-domain tuning,
Micro-F1=0.571)—provides evidence for model-level
generalization with preserved AUROC (all > 0.93)
on human-validated labels. Calibrated transfer (fold-
9 thresholds, Micro-F1=0.681) shows performance re-
covery via standard recalibration, and best possible
(oracle, Micro-F1=0.694) establishes the upper bound.
PR>200ms rule baseline via NeuroKit2 delineation
(AUROC=0.783, sensitivity=0.873) identifies PR pro-
longation while ResNet (AUROC=0.937, ∆ = +0.154)
captures additional discriminative information.

6) Statistical rigor: Multi-seed training (3 seeds ×
2 patient splits) showed training stability (Micro-F1
SD=0.0025), with bootstrap CIs (n = 1, 000) and De-
Long tests providing complementary statistical evidence
for model comparisons.

7) Handcrafted vs deep learning comparison: Direct
comparison on identical patient-level splits across three
feature regimes (simple, clinical, raw signal).

II. METHODS

A. Dataset

CODE-15%: Brazilian ECG dataset with 345,797 12-lead
recordings (400Hz, 10-second duration) from 233,771 patients.
Target conditions: 1AVB (1.65%), CRBBB (2.80%), CLBBB
(1.74%), SBRAD (1.62%), AFIB (2.03%).

Label source: Labels were derived from the CODE
dataset’s automated ECG interpretation system, which assigns
diagnostic codes based on algorithmic analysis of ECG fea-
tures. These labels represent the automated diagnostic output
rather than physician-confirmed diagnoses. Multi-label classi-
fication is supported: among the 5 evaluated conditions, 93.8%
of samples have zero positive labels, 5.2% have exactly one,



IEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 4

and 1.0% have two or more. The most common co-occurrence
is CRBBB+1AVB (0.33% of samples). One-vs-rest evaluation
treats each disease independently; micro-F1 pools all per-
sample predictions equally while macro-F1 averages per-
disease F1 scores.

Patient-level split: 60% train (207,232 samples), 20% vali-
dation (69,045 samples), 20% test (69,520 samples). Random
seed 42 for reproducibility. Patient-level splitting ensures no
patient appears in multiple splits, preventing data leakage from
patient-specific patterns.

B. Approach 1: XGBoost + Simple Summary Features (98D)

Feature extraction (98 dimensions):
• Rhythm features (14): RR intervals

(Mean/Std/Min/Max/Median/Range), HR (Mean/Std),
HRV (RMSSD/SDNN/pNN50/CV), RR Irregularity,
QRS Count

• Amplitude features (84): Per-lead statistics
(Mean/Std/Min/Max/Range/RMS/PeakToPeak) for
12 leads

Note on feature limitations: These features are intention-
ally simple summary statistics. They do NOT include com-
prehensive clinical ECG measurements such as QRS duration,
PR interval, QT interval, QRS axis, P-wave duration, T-wave
morphology, or fiducial point timing (P/QRS/T onset/offset).
Comprehensive feature sets like PTB-XL+ [6] include 166
such measurements but require complex fiducial detection. Our
goal is to identify limitations of simple features to motivate
both clinical feature engineering and deep learning approaches.

Model: XGBoost with one-vs-rest strategy per disease.
Hyperparameters (nestimators = 100, max depth = 8,
learning rate = 0.1) were selected via 5-fold cross-
validation on the training set, searching over max depth ∈
{4, 6, 8, 10} and learning rate ∈ {0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2}, with
nestimators determined by early stopping (patience=10 on val-
idation log-loss). scale pos weight was set inversely pro-
portional to class prevalence for class balancing. The same
hyperparameter search protocol was applied to all feature sets
(rhythm-only, amplitude-only, combined, clinical-MVP).

Threshold tuning: Per-label optimal thresholds were se-
lected on the validation set by maximizing F1 score. The
same protocol was applied identically to all methods: for each
disease, we swept 50 candidate thresholds uniformly spaced
between 0.01 and 0.99 on the validation set and selected the
threshold that maximized per-disease F1. The tuned thresholds
were then applied to the test set.

C. Approach 2: XGBoost + Clinical-MVP Features (110D)

To test whether adding AV conduction timing features
closes the 1AVB detection gap, we designed a Clinical-MVP
(Clinically Meaningful Vital Parameters) feature set organized
into four physiological blocks:

Block 1—Rhythm & Rate (11 features): Heart rate
(mean, std, min, max), RR interval statistics (mean, std, min,
max, median, range), and RR variability (RMSSD, SDNN,
CV, pNN50, RR irregularity index). Computed from R-peak
positions detected via NeuroKit2’s Elgendi algorithm [8].

Block 2—AV Conduction Timing (12 features): PR in-
terval (mean, std, min, max, median), PR segment duration,
and P-wave duration metrics. P-waves were detected as the
maximum amplitude point in an 80–200ms window preceding
each R-peak (Lead II), with PR interval computed as the
temporal distance from P-wave peak to subsequent R-peak
[9]. Physiological constraints (PR ∈ [80, 400]ms, P-wave
∈ [60, 140]ms) were applied to filter implausible detections.

Block 3—QRS Morphology & Conduction (8 features):
QRS duration (mean, std, min, max) estimated from gradient
zero-crossings around R-peaks; QRS frontal axis computed
from net deflection in leads I and aVF [10]; R/S amplitude
ratio per lead (mean, std); and terminal S-wave amplitude.

Block 4—Signal Quality (4 features): Baseline wander
index (low-frequency power ratio), signal-to-noise ratio, lead
dropout count, and electrode contact quality score computed
from the coefficient of variation across leads.

Additionally, per-lead amplitude statistics (72 features:
mean, std, min, max, range, RMS for 12 leads) were included,
matching the amplitude block from the simple feature set.
Total: 35 clinical features + 72 amplitude features + 3
metadata features = 110 dimensions.

Implementation: Feature extraction used NeuroKit2 [8]
exclusively for R-peak detection (fast, ∼2ms/sample), with
custom SciPy signal processing for P-wave detection, QRS
duration estimation, QRS axis computation, and R/S ratio cal-
culation. This hybrid approach achieved ∼50 samples/second
extraction speed, processing all 345,797 samples in approxi-
mately 2 hours.

D. Approach 3: 1D ResNet on Raw Signals

Architecture:
• Input: Raw 12-lead ECG (12 × 4096), z-score normal-

ized per lead
• Preprocessing: Original signals (4000 samples at 400Hz,

10s duration) were resampled to 4096 samples via linear
interpolation, extending the temporal window to 10.24s.
This preserves the full 10s recording while providing a
power-of-two input length compatible with 4× downsam-
pling stages.

• Backbone: 4 ResNet stages with residual blocks:
– Stage 1: 2 blocks, 64 channels, kernel=7, stride=2
– Stage 2: 2 blocks, 128 channels, kernel=7, stride=2
– Stage 3: 2 blocks, 256 channels, kernel=7, stride=2
– Stage 4: 2 blocks, 512 channels, kernel=7, stride=2

• Residual block: Conv1D → BatchNorm → ReLU →
Conv1D → BatchNorm → skip connection → ReLU

• Pooling: AdaptiveAvgPool1D(1) → flatten to 512-dim
vector

• Classifier: Dropout(0.2) → Linear(512 → 5) → Sigmoid
• Loss: BCEWithLogitsLoss with per-class weights (in-

verse prevalence)
• Parameters: 1.2M trainable parameters
• Complexity: 0.8 GFLOPs per sample
Training: Adam optimizer (lr=0.001), ReduceLROn-

Plateau scheduler (factor=0.5, patience=5), early stopping
(patience=10 on validation loss), batch size 64, trained for



IEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 5

up to 50 epochs (early stopping typically triggered at epoch
23–28). Training time: 2.5 hours on A100 GPU (single run).

Multi-seed training: To assess statistical robustness, we
trained 4 independent ResNet runs: 3 with different model
initialization seeds (42, 123, 456) on the primary patient
split (seed=42), and 1 on a second independent patient split
(seed=123) with model seed 42. All other hyperparameters
were identical. This enables estimation of both within-split
variance (model seed sensitivity) and cross-split generalization
(patient split sensitivity).

Competitive DL baseline—SE-ResNet: To address
whether modern architectural enhancements provide additional
benefit, we trained an SE-ResNet-1D (Squeeze-and-Excitation
ResNet) with identical architecture, hyperparameters,
and data splits as the baseline ResNet. SE blocks
add channel-wise attention after each residual block:
AdaptiveAvgPool1d → Linear(C, C//16) →
ReLU → Linear(C//16, C) → Sigmoid →
channel-wise multiply, introducing 87K additional
parameters (1.3M total). The SE reduction ratio was set to 16
following standard practice [7]. Training converged at epoch
10 (early stopping, best val Micro-F1=0.7410).

Competitive DL baseline—Lightweight 1D Transformer:
To test whether a patch-based self-attention architecture pro-
vides advantages over the convolutional ResNet for ECG sig-
nals, we trained a lightweight 1D transformer with an identical
conv stem (Conv1d(12→64, k=15, s=2) → BN → ReLU →
MaxPool(k=3, s=2)), producing 64-channel × 1024-length
features. A patch embedding layer (Conv1d(64→160, k=16,
s=16)) partitioned features into 64 patches of dimension
160. A learnable CLS token was prepended, and learnable
1D position embeddings were added. A 4-layer Transformer
encoder (d=160, heads=8, MLP ratio=4, gelu activation, pre-
norm, dropout=0.1) processed the sequence, and the CLS
token output was fed to a linear classifier (160→5). Total
parameters: 1,424,293 (comparable to ResNet’s 1.2M). Train-
ing used the identical protocol as ResNet: Adam (lr=0.001),
ReduceLROnPlateau (factor=0.5, patience=3), early stopping
(patience=10 on validation loss), batch size 128. Training
completed 50 epochs (val Micro-F1=0.6168, no early stop
triggered).

Threshold tuning: Same validation-based approach as XG-
Boost.

E. PR-Window Occlusion Experiment

To test whether ResNet relies on PR-segment information
for 1AVB detection, we performed a counterfactual occlusion
experiment:

Hypothesis: If ResNet uses PR-segment timing for 1AVB
classification, occluding the PR segment should cause a larger
degradation in 1AVB prediction probability than occluding a
control region of equal length.

Sample selection: All 1AVB-positive samples from the
test set (n = 1, 084) plus an equal number of matched
1AVB-negative controls (n = 1, 084), totaling 2,168 samples.
Samples with fewer than 3 detectable R-peaks were excluded
(54 samples, 2.5%).

Occlusion conditions (within-subject design):
1) PR-window occlusion: For each heartbeat, a 160ms

window centered at (R peak − 120ms) was set to zero,
targeting the PR segment including the P-wave and PR
interval

2) ST-segment occlusion (anatomical control): A 160ms
window centered at (R peak + 80ms) was set to zero,
targeting the ST segment which should be irrelevant for
1AVB detection

3) Random-window occlusion (spatial control): A ran-
dom 160ms window (excluding QRS) was set to zero

4) Clean (baseline): Original unmodified signal
Measurement: For each condition, we computed the

ResNet-predicted 1AVB probability for every sample. The
primary metric was the paired probability change (∆prob)
on 1AVB-positive samples: ∆prob = p(1AVB | clean) −
p(1AVB | occluded). Positive ∆prob indicates the model
reduced its 1AVB confidence when that segment was occluded.

Bootstrap CI: 95% confidence intervals on paired effects
were computed via patient-level bootstrap (n = 1, 000 itera-
tions).

F. Extended Perturbation Experiments

To validate additional disease-specific pathways beyond
PR-segment/1AVB, we performed two additional perturbation
experiments:

QRS occlusion → BBB (CRBBB + CLBBB): For BBB-
positive samples (n = 3, 184) and matched negative controls
(n = 3, 184), a 160ms window centered at each R-peak
was zero-masked across all 12 leads. The QRS complex
is clinically diagnostic for BBB (widened QRS > 120ms,
characteristic rSR′ pattern). Two anatomical controls followed
the same protocol: ST-segment occlusion (160ms at R peak
+ 40ms) and random-window occlusion (160ms excluding
QRS). The same R-peak detection, matched-subset protocol,
and patient-level paired bootstrap (n = 1, 000) were used as
in the PR occlusion experiment.

RR regularization → AFIB: For AFIB-positive samples
(n = 1, 256) and matched negative controls (n = 1, 256),
each heartbeat (bounded by midpoints between consecutive
R-peaks) was time-warped to the median RR interval length,
preserving per-beat QRS morphology while destroying RR-
interval irregularity. Beat-order permutation served as a func-
tional control: beats were randomly permuted, preserving the
set of RR intervals but destroying their temporal order. If
ResNet relies on RR irregularity for AFIB detection, RR
regularization should cause greater degradation than beat per-

H. Frozen-Model External Validation

To assess model-level generalization, the CODE-trained 1D
ResNet was applied without fine-tuning to PTB-XL [4] raw
12-lead signals. PTB-XL contains 21,799 10-second 12-lead
ECGs from 18,885 patients at 500Hz (PhysioNet). Official
patient-level folds were used: folds 1–8 for reference, fold
9 (n = 2, 183) for threshold recalibration, and fold 10
(n = 2, 198) for testing. Fold 10 labels are fully human-
validated by cardiologists.

Preprocessing: Signals were downsampled from 500Hz to
400Hz via Fourier resampling to match CODE-15% input
rate, then trimmed/padded to 4,096 samples (10.24s). Z-score
normalization was applied per lead. Lead order (I, II, III, AVR,
AVL, AVF, V1–V6) matched CODE-15% ordering.

Label mapping: SCP-ECG diagnostic codes were mapped
to the 5 target diseases using strict primary code matching
(same mapping as Section 2.7 cross-dataset validation). Only
fold 10 labels are human-validated.

PR rule baseline: To test for label circularity, PR inter-
vals were computed using NeuroKit2’s wavelet-based ECG
delineation (ecg_delineate, peaks method) on the original
500Hz signal. P-wave onsets identified via wavelet decom-
position of the P-QRS-T complex; PR interval measured as
R-peak to P-onset time per beat (median across valid beats,
physiological bounds 80–400ms). PR>200ms threshold yields
binary predictions; PR interval as continuous score yields
AUROC. DeLong test compares ResNet AUROC against PR
interval AUROC.

Evaluation: Identical protocol to CODE-15% test set eval-
uation. Thresholds were recalibrated on fold 9 (F1-max per
disease). Bootstrap CIs (n = 1, 000, patient-level) and DeLong
tests were computed. Total inference time: approximately 5
minutes on a single GPU.

F. Statistical Robustness Analysis (Bootstrap CI)

We performed patient-level bootstrap resampling (n = 1000
iterations) to assess statistical robustness. In each iteration, we
resampled patients with replacement and computed predictions
on all samples from the resampled patient set. All metrics (F1,
AUROC, AUPRC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV) were
recomputed from predictions, with per-label thresholds fixed at
the values tuned on the original validation set. 95% confidence
intervals were obtained via the percentile method (2.5th and
97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap distribution).

Clinical interpretation of PPV/NPV: Positive Predictive
Value (PPV) and Negative Predictive Value (NPV) answer: “If
the model predicts positive/negative, what is the probability the
patient truly has/doesn’t have the disease?”

Key findings:
1) Low prevalence limits PPV: All diseases have low

prevalence (1.6–2.8%), resulting in moderate PPV even
with high sensitivity/specificity. This is a fundamental
challenge in rare disease detection.

2) 1AVB shows dramatic PPV improvement: XGBoost
Simple PPV=0.059 (only 5.9% of positive predictions
are correct) vs ResNet PPV=0.529 (52.9% correct)
→ 9× improvement. This indicates ResNet’s superior
ability to reduce false positives for this challenging
condition.

3) NPV universally high (> 98.5%): Due to low preva-
lence, negative predictions are highly reliable for both
models. This is clinically valuable for ruling out disease.

4) ResNet consistently improves PPV: Across all dis-
eases, ResNet achieves higher PPV than XGBoost Sim-
ple, reducing false positive burden in clinical workflows.
